forces.title: Elevated bond yields drive corporate shift to bank financing
forces.description: High corporate bond yields have reduced the attractiveness of market borrowings, prompting large corporates, infrastructure developers, and NBFCs to increasingly rely on bank financing for incremental funding, refinancing, and working capital needs. This shift makes bank credit more competitive and boosts corporate lending volumes for banks, particularly in industrial and infrastructure sectors, as companies seek more favorable terms compared to capital market alternatives.

forces.title: Strong credit demand from industrial and infrastructure sectors
forces.description: Industrial credit growth accelerated to 15.1% y-o-y in April 2026, driven by higher working capital requirements in sectors like infrastructure, engineering, metals, chemicals, and petroleum. Infrastructure lending specifically grew by 10.1% y-o-y, led by power and ports, signaling improving project execution and investment activity. This broad-based demand supports corporate lending, indicating robust economic activity that necessitates significant bank financing for various projects and operational needs.

forces.title: Geopolitical tensions risk MSME and export-linked credit quality
forces.description: The ongoing West Asia conflict introduces uncertainty for bank credit to MSMEs and export-oriented sectors. Disruptions in trade flows, elongated receivable cycles, elevated input/logistics costs, and tightening working capital positions could pressure cash flows. While current stress is limited, the actual impact from these external factors may materialize in Q2FY27/H2FY27. This could lead to more conservative underwriting standards across the banking system and negatively affect trade finance portfolios, increasing credit risk.

forces.title: Easing bond yields could moderate bank credit growth
forces.description: The current strong bank credit growth is partly attributable to corporates favoring bank financing over market borrowings due to elevated bond yields. Any future easing in bond market yields or improvement in capital market funding conditions could encourage NBFCs and large corporates to shift back towards market borrowings. This potential reversal of funding preference would likely temper the pace of bank credit growth, particularly impacting lending to NBFCs and large industries as capital markets regain attractiveness for fundraising.

forces.title: Broad-based improvement in corporate asset quality
forces.description: Public Sector Banks (PSBs) and Private Sector Banks (PVBs) exhibited broad-based improvement in sectoral asset quality, with Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratios declining across corporate, MSME, and agriculture segments. This positive trend is driven by sustained recoveries, lower incremental stress formation, prudent underwriting practices, and ongoing resolution of legacy stressed assets. Resilient domestic asset quality, supported by stable corporate balance sheets, provides a strong foundation and reduces risk for corporate lending activities.

forces.title: ECL framework to impact corporate lending risk appetite
forces.description: The transition to the Expected Credit Loss (ECL) framework is a positive structural development for the Indian banking system, enhancing transparency and risk sensitivity. However, under ECL norms, any shift towards higher-yielding but riskier corporate assets could necessitate disproportionately higher provisions. This will increase the importance of Stage 2 assets and could potentially offset margin gains and compress returns on total assets. This fundamental change will significantly influence corporate lending strategy and banks' risk appetite for various loan segments.

forces.title: Strong capital adequacy supports robust credit expansion
forces.description: Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) maintain strong capital adequacy, with median Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) ratios at 16.2% and Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) at 17.9% in Q4FY26, well above regulatory requirements. This robust capital base, supported by healthy internal accruals and strategic bond issuances, provides significant headroom for credit growth. Public Sector Banks, with their relatively lower Credit-to-Deposit (CD) ratios, possess particular capacity for further credit expansion, which directly benefits corporate lending volumes and transaction banking capabilities.

forces.title: Generative AI for enhanced credit appraisal and underwriting
forces.description: Seven public sector banks have introduced 32 generative AI applications across credit appraisal, underwriting, and risk management processes. This initiative aims to strengthen operational efficiency, accelerate decision-making, and improve governance. For corporate lending, AI-driven credit underwriting promises higher accuracy in default prediction, faster time-to-decision, and lower processing costs. This innovation allows for more granular credit models, potentially expanding the addressable lending market to smaller ticket sizes and asset-light businesses traditionally deemed uneconomical.

forces.title: Buoyant IPO market with strong fundraising pipeline
forces.description: India experienced a record IPO year in 2025, with fundraising reaching approximately Rs. 1.95 lakh crore across 365 IPOs. A robust pipeline of over Rs. 4 lakh crore is projected for 2026, reflecting strong investor confidence and increasing retail participation in capital markets. This vibrant activity creates significant opportunities for investment banks in managing Equity Capital Market (ECM) transactions, including IPOs, and driving substantial fee income for advisory and arrangement services.

forces.title: Unified Lending Interface to democratize private sector credit
forces.description: The Unified Lending Interface (ULI) aims to democratize access to credit for the private sector by streamlining the loan application and disbursal process. This initiative is expected to simplify and expedite corporate lending, particularly for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), by leveraging India’s Digital Public Infrastructure. The ULI will drive credit access, reduce processing times, and potentially increase the volume of corporate loans, opening up new avenues for growth in wholesale banking services.

forces.title: Increased investments in digital infrastructure and AI for banking
forces.description: Banks are significantly increasing investments in data analytics, generative AI capabilities, digital infrastructure, and broader technology transformation initiatives. These investments aim to enhance operational efficiency, improve customer service, and streamline internal processes, including credit appraisal, underwriting, and risk management in corporate banking. This shift will reshape how corporate and investment banking functions are delivered, reducing costs, improving decision-making speed, and fostering innovation in product and service offerings for wholesale clients.

forces.title: Policy support for financial services and credit access
forces.description: Government policies are strongly supporting India’s financial services sector through banking reforms, digital initiatives like UPI-based credit, and expanded financial inclusion schemes. These measures aim to improve credit access, enhance efficiency, and ensure sector stability by leveraging technology and regulatory frameworks. Such supportive policies create a conducive environment for corporate lending, trade finance, and broader investment banking activities, facilitating business growth and ensuring robust operational backbones for financial institutions.

viewpoints.title: Strong corporate advance growth across diverse sectors
viewpoints.description: Scheduled Commercial Banks reported 15.3% y-o-y growth in net advances in Q4FY26, with corporate advances demonstrating robust expansion. This growth is significantly driven by emerging opportunities and increased credit demand from diverse sectors including electronics, food processing, automobiles, renewable energy, and semiconductors. The trend is further supported by reduced competition from the bond market, which encourages corporates to seek bank financing for working capital and project execution, ensuring continued momentum in corporate lending.

viewpoints.title: Banking asset quality resilient despite emerging geopolitical risks
viewpoints.description: The Indian banking sector's asset quality continued its improvement trajectory in Q4FY26, with the Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratio reaching a multi-year low of 1.8%. Public Sector Banks, in particular, showed broad-based asset quality improvement across corporate, MSME, and agriculture segments. While overall domestic asset quality remains resilient, geopolitical tensions in West Asia present monitorable risks for MSME and export-linked sectors. Potential stress from these external factors may materialize in Q2FY27/H2FY27, indicating a need for continued vigilance in corporate lending portfolios.

viewpoints.title: Credit growth driven by corporate shift to bank financing
viewpoints.description: Non-food bank credit remained strong at 15.8% y-o-y in April 2026, primarily due to large corporates and NBFCs shifting from market borrowings to bank financing. Elevated corporate bond yields reduced the relative attractiveness of commercial paper (CP) and corporate bond issuances, prompting greater reliance on bank credit for industrial and infrastructure sectors. This indicates a positive compositional shift for corporate lending within banks, as it captures a larger share of the overall funding market. However, it's driven by funding dynamics rather than a sharp pickup in underlying demand and could reverse if market conditions change.

viewpoints.title: Robust capital buffers support sustained bank credit growth
viewpoints.description: Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) maintained strong capital adequacy in Q4FY26, with their median Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) increasing to 17.9% and Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) ratios improving. This robust capital base, significantly augmented by healthy internal capital accruals and strategic bond issuances, provides substantial headroom for future credit expansion. Public Sector Banks, with their relatively lower Credit-to-Deposit (CD) ratios, possess particular capacity for further corporate lending growth, reinforcing the sector's ability to support economic activity and expansion.
